opening.title: A project can contain smaller projects
keyPoints: A Step has one duration.
A Group can contain steps and groups.
Ask the same minutes question of a part or whole.
opening.narration: A work planner starts with three steps: ten minutes, twenty minutes, and five minutes. Adding them is easy. The next requirement says that the first two steps belong to a smaller group, and that this group belongs to the larger project alongside the five-minute step. Later there may be more levels. The total should still be thirty-five. Before choosing a pattern, notice the repeating question: how much time is beneath this item? That question makes sense for both one step and an entire project. The chapter allows zero minutes and empty groups, and rejects totals above ten thousand. Those edge rules are part of the design.
actions: Sketch the project with one inner group and three leaves.
Ask which question is meaningful at every node.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → A flat list works until a task contains tasks

question.prompt: What common operation is meaningful for both a step and a group?
question.answer: Return the total duration beneath that object; a step returns its own duration and a group combines child durations.

opening.title: Start with a flat list and an ordinary loop
keyPoints: A vector stores the flat durations.
A range loop adds each value once.
Bound checks happen before addition.
opening.narration: A flat list does not need a class hierarchy. This program stores integer durations in a vector and uses a range-based loop to visit each one. The colon means take each value from durations in order. Here n is a copied integer, which is small and has no ownership issue. The checks reject a negative duration and prevent the running total from crossing the allowed budget. For this fixed valid list, the output is thirty-five. The loop is an honest starting point because the data is flat. We should preserve its simple add-once reasoning when the data later becomes nested.
actions: Explain why checking n > 10000 - total comes before total += n.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch08.json → A flat list works until a task contains tasks

question.prompt: Why not start by adding then checking whether the result exceeds the budget?
question.answer: Checking first preserves the bounded arithmetic invariant and avoids relying on an addition that may become unsafe under broader bounds.

opening.title: A shallow traversal silently misses work
keyPoints: The input now has children below children.
One loop sees only the root and immediate children.
A recursive function follows all valid levels.
opening.narration: To model the new nesting requirement safely, this small demonstration introduces a Node with a local duration and a vector of child nodes. It is a value-based alternative, not the chapter's polymorphic Work family. The shallow loop adds only immediate child values, so it prints five and misses the ten and twenty below the inner group. The recursive function solves the same question for each child and prints thirty-five. Recursion means applying the operation to a smaller part until there are no children left. All input here is fixed, finite, nonnegative, and within budget; the demonstration isolates the depth error rather than claiming general input validation.
actions: Mark exactly which nodes the shallow loop visits.
Predict the two outputs before running.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch08.json → A flat list works until a task contains tasks

question.prompt: Why does the shallow result equal five?
question.answer: The inner group contributes its local zero, and its ten- and twenty-minute descendants are never visited.

opening.title: One question, two kinds of answer
keyPoints: Work defines minutes().
Step answers directly.
Group asks its children and combines their answers.
opening.narration: Now we can explain the chapter's choice. Composite gives individual items and containers one useful contract over a tree. Work supplies minutes. Step holds a checked duration and returns it. Group holds children that are themselves Work objects and adds their answers. A child may therefore be another group without changing the parent's loop. The value-based Node demonstration remains a reasonable alternative when one data representation is enough. The Work family becomes useful when distinct kinds of work need their own implementations while callers keep one query. We do not add child-editing operations to every Work merely to make every class look alike.
actions: Point to the recursion and the runtime type selection as separate mechanisms.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → One operation for a part and a whole

question.prompt: Does Composite require every leaf to support adding children?
question.answer: No. Keep only meaningful common operations on Work; adding children can remain a Group-specific construction concern.

mechanism.title: Recursion and virtual dispatch do different jobs
keyPoints: The recursive call follows the tree.
Virtual dispatch chooses Step or Group behavior.
A leaf or empty group stops the descent.
mechanism.narration: Two mechanisms cooperate in the chapter, and each answers a different question. Recursion says to ask a child the same minutes question. Virtual dispatch decides which implementation answers for that child object. A Step returns immediately. A Group enters another loop and asks its own children. On a finite acyclic tree, repeated descent eventually reaches a leaf or an empty group. A tree means that following child links cannot lead back to an ancestor. Without that rule, repeated calls might never finish. The ordinary bottom-up construction in this program supports the tree rule, but a future editing API would need to preserve it explicitly.
actions: Trace one leaf call and one child-group call from the same loop.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → One operation for a part and a whole

question.prompt: What stops recursion for an empty Group?
question.answer: Its loop has no iterations, so its local total remains zero and returns immediately.

theory.what: One query works recursively for leaves and containers.
theory.why: Callers should not hard-code a separate loop for every depth.
theory.invariant: The child relation is finite and acyclic.
theory.risk: A cycle introduced by unsafe editing can prevent termination.

mechanism.title: Each recursive call owns its own subtotal
keyPoints: Outer total starts at zero.
Inner group computes ten plus twenty.
Outer group receives thirty, then adds five.
mechanism.narration: Do not picture one total variable being passed around the whole tree. Every call to Group::minutes creates its own local total. The outer call pauses while the inner group computes thirty using a different local variable. Once the inner call returns, its local storage ends and the returned integer becomes available to the outer call. The outer call adds that thirty, then asks its second child for five. This explains why setting total to zero at the start of each call is correct. Storing one shared running total in a member could make repeated queries accumulate old work or make concurrent queries interfere.
actions: Draw two call frames with separate total boxes.
Run the query twice and predict why both answers remain thirty-five.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Follow the return values, not just the arrows

question.prompt: Would resetting the inner total erase the outer total?
question.answer: No. They are separate local variables in separate active calls.

theory.what: Every group computes and returns an independent subtotal.
theory.where: The local total variable inside Group::minutes.
theory.why: A child result must combine cleanly into its parent result.
theory.invariant: Each child contributes exactly once per query.
theory.risk: A stored running total can retain old values across repeated queries.

mechanism.title: Ownership follows the same tree shape
keyPoints: Children owns unique_ptr<Work> handles.
Each handle owns one child object.
Destroying the root destroys the owned subtree.
mechanism.narration: Children is a type alias: a shorter name for a vector of unique_ptr values that own Work objects. The vector owns those handles, and each handle is responsible for deleting one child. A child Group repeats the ownership arrangement below itself. Moving a finished vector into Group transfers those owners without copying the work objects. Std::move permits this transfer; it does not prove that the moved-from vector is empty, and this program does not depend on that. Work has a virtual destructor so deletion through the base type reaches the correct Step or Group destructor. The root therefore controls the complete subtree lifetime.
actions: Follow cleanup from the outer Group through its vector and each child owner.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Build ownership from the leaves upward

question.prompt: Why is copying Children disallowed by its ownership type?
question.answer: Its unique_ptr elements represent exclusive ownership, so copying them would incorrectly create two exclusive owners.

theory.what: A group exclusively owns its child objects through movable handles.
theory.why: The tree should clean itself up without a manual deletion traversal.
theory.invariant: Each owned node has one exclusive owning path.
theory.risk: Creating a second unique_ptr from an already-owned raw pointer violates the ownership rule.

mechanism.title: Validate the topology and the arithmetic
keyPoints: Group rejects a null child during construction.
Step accepts only zero through ten thousand.
Group rejects an excessive subtotal before adding.
mechanism.narration: The tree contract contains more than correct class names. A null child would make the arrow call invalid, so Group rejects it while taking ownership. If construction throws, completed member objects clean up automatically, including their unique owners. During a query, the duration contract says each child returns a nonnegative value. Group tests whether the next contribution exceeds the remaining budget before addition. The thrown overflow_error describes the project's budget rejection here, not evidence that signed integer overflow already happened. If a future Work implementation returns negative minutes, it can violate this reasoning even though its override compiles. New implementations must honor the same semantic range.
actions: Trace children of ten thousand and one and locate the throw before addition.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Follow the return values, not just the arrows

question.prompt: Why is a child returning negative minutes a contract problem rather than a formatting problem?
question.answer: The nonnegative range is required for meaningful durations and for the remaining-budget arithmetic.

theory.what: Construction and queries enforce distinct structural and numeric rules.
theory.where: Group constructor, Step constructor, and Group::minutes.
theory.why: Valid object links and bounded values are both needed for a trustworthy total.
theory.invariant: Children are non-null and every returned duration is within the common contract.
theory.risk: A new derived type can compile while violating the allowed result range.

mechanism.title: Const references make the child loop readable
keyPoints: const auto& borrows each stored owner.
child->minutes() follows the owner to Work.
steps() is a second query, not a replacement for time.
mechanism.narration: Read the child loop from left to right. Const auto ampersand declares a read-only reference to each element already stored in the vector. Auto lets the compiler infer the unique_ptr type, and the reference avoids trying to copy an exclusive owner. The arrow follows that pointer to the Work object and calls minutes. The lab adds steps with the same structural recursion but a different meaning: a zero-minute Step still counts as one leaf. Do not derive leaf count from duration, because zero is a valid duration. Each full traversal visits each node once, and active recursive calls grow with the nesting depth.
actions: Compare an empty Group with Step(0): same minutes, different leaf counts.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Cost, depth, and the limits of uniform operations

question.prompt: Why cannot steps() be computed by counting only positive durations?
question.answer: A valid zero-minute Step must count as one leaf, while an empty Group has no leaves.

comparisons.label: Polymorphic Work tree
comparisons.text: Distinct types provide one shared query; ownership is explicit.

comparisons.label: Value-based Node tree
comparisons.text: One representation can be simpler when every node follows the same rules.

comparisons.label: Cached total
comparisons.text: Can reduce repeated queries, but editing later requires a correct update policy.

closing.title: Uniform does not mean every action fits
keyPoints: Total duration applies to leaves and groups.
Adding children does not apply to a leaf.
Keep specialized edits outside the shared query.
closing.narration: A common mistake is to put every possible operation on the shared base because the pattern promises uniform use. Uniformity is useful only for operations whose meanings remain clear. Minutes has a natural answer for a Step and a Group. Add-child does not have a natural meaning for a Step, so a do-nothing implementation would hide a programming mistake. The chapter instead takes a finished child list during Group construction. If editing becomes necessary, give editing a separate design with ownership and cycle rules. The fact that two objects share a query does not mean they should share every command.
actions: Ask learners to classify total duration, leaf duration editing, and subtree export as shared or specialized operations.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → One operation for a part and a whole

question.prompt: Why is a leaf add-child method that silently does nothing harmful?
question.answer: It makes an apparently successful edit discard the request and gives callers a misleading common contract.

closing.title: Depth and width create different risks
keyPoints: A query does work proportional to nodes visited.
Its recursive stack grows with depth.
Untrusted nesting requires an explicit limit or iterative traversal.
closing.narration: A large tree can be wide, deep, or both. A million direct leaf children create a long loop, but only a small number of nested calls. A million groups inside one another create a very deep call chain and can exhaust the stack. The chapter demonstrates a small trusted tree; it does not promise safe traversal of arbitrary untrusted input depth. A file parser that builds these objects should enforce a depth limit, or the query can be redesigned to use an explicit stack. Notice that validation belongs where the risky input enters. Timing a tiny example does not establish a bound for every tree shape.
actions: Compare a shallow wide tree with a narrow deep tree using the same node count.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Cost, depth, and the limits of uniform operations

question.prompt: Why does a node-count limit alone not describe stack use precisely?
question.answer: Trees with equal node counts can have very different maximum depths; recursive stack use follows depth.

closing.title: Reconstruct Composite from the work plan
keyPoints: State the shared meaningful operation.
Name the stopping cases.
Explain ownership and one preserved invariant.
closing.narration: Without looking at the source, explain why one client can ask for the minutes of a Step or a project. Then name the two stopping cases: a Step and an empty Group. Finally, explain how the returned subtotals differ from the owning pointers that keep the tree alive. These three explanations cover behavior, control, and lifetime. To transfer the idea, consider a folder-size tool. A file can return its byte count and a folder can sum children, but links and cycles may change the tree assumption. Reusing a pattern responsibly includes checking whether the new domain keeps the original structural promises.
actions: Have learners explain the folder example and identify what symbolic links could change.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch08.json → Cost, depth, and the limits of uniform operations

question.prompt: What must be reconsidered when a supposed tree can link back to an ancestor?
question.answer: Termination and ownership assumptions; traversal needs a policy for cycles rather than blindly recurring forever.
